content.p: On the night of Saturday 18 June 1994, two gunmen walked into a small pub in a quiet County Down village and opened fire on men who were watching a football match. Six Catholic men died in the Heights Bar in Loughinisland; five others were wounded. The Ulster Volunteer Force, a loyalist paramilitary group, claimed responsibility. More than three decades later no one has been convicted.

The case is remembered for what happened afterwards as much as for the shooting. A Police Ombudsman's report in 2011 found no collusion and was thrown out by the High Court. A second report in 2016 concluded that collusion between some police officers and the UVF was a "significant feature" of the murders. In between, and after, the families fought a long campaign, two journalists who told the story on film were arrested, and a court ruled that an Ombudsman had gone further than the law allowed him.
content.h2: A mixed village on World Cup night
content.p: Loughinisland sits about a kilometre from the main road between Belfast and Newcastle. The Irish Times described it in 2014 as a farming community where, until that night, people thought of the Troubles as something that happened elsewhere. Aidan O'Toole, whose family owns the Heights and who was behind the bar that evening, said the village was "a mixed community" where Protestants and Catholics "got on well", and that the pub had always had both in it. The six dead men were all Catholic; the Irish Times called that a fluke, and O'Toole's own words were that the bar was "just a Catholic-owned bar and an easy target".

The game on the television was Ireland against Italy at the 1994 World Cup in the United States. Ireland won, one goal to nil, in New Jersey. Adrian Rogan had gone to the bar that day to collect two tickets for an Ulster championship match the next day; the tickets were handed back to his wife Claire with his belongings.

According to the Irish Times, about an hour of the match had been played when two men in boiler suits and balaclavas came in, shouted a sectarian slur and fired with AK-47 rifles. The paper counted fifteen men in the bar. The Independent, writing the next day, put the time at about 10.20 p.m. and said the gunmen drove off in a red car before they could be identified. Five victims died at the scene and a sixth later in hospital, the paper said, and it first counted four injured; later reports, including the Police Ombudsman's, say five.

Adrian Rogan was 34, Patrick O'Hare 35, Eamon Byrne 39 and Barney Green 87. With them died Malcolm Jenkinson and Daniel McCreanor. Green was one of the oldest victims of the Troubles, one report said. Reports differ on two of the others: the Irish Times gave McCreanor, Green's nephew, and Jenkinson as both 54, while the Ombudsman's office, ITV and the BBC gave Jenkinson as 53 and McCreanor as 59. Byrne and O'Hare were brothers-in-law.

The attack came in a week of violence. The Independent set it alongside the Greysteel killings of the previous October and, the day before, the killing of a Protestant man, Cecil James Dougherty, in an attack on a workmen's hut at Newtownabbey. The Irish Times recorded that the IRA declared a ceasefire on 1 September 1994 and that loyalist groups followed about six weeks later.

No one was charged. The Irish Times says a dozen people were arrested and questioned; the BBC said in 2012 that 16 had been arrested. A senior RUC officer had told Claire Rogan that "no stone would be left unturned". Over the years the families came to doubt that. They learned, the Irish Times reported, that few of those arrested had been properly tested for samples or DNA, and that the getaway car, a Triumph Acclaim found the day after the killings, had sat in a police yard before being sent to a scrapyard to be crushed because it took up space.

The families, among them Adrian Rogan's daughter Emma, hired a solicitor, compared notes at the Heights and complained to the Police Ombudsman for Northern Ireland. They suspected the RUC investigation had been undermined to protect informants.

The first Ombudsman, Al Hutchinson, reported in June 2011. The BBC described the families as strongly critical of it, and the families called it a whitewash. The Irish Times noted that although the report found major police failings, it found no evidence of collusion and did not mention Special Branch at all. The families challenged it in the High Court, which quashed it. The BBC reported this on 19 December 2012. Hutchinson was replaced by Michael Maguire, who took over a fresh investigation. The BBC said his decision to reopen the case was believed to relate to statements from a self-confessed UVF informer and a former RUC detective.

Maguire published on 9 June 2016. His report ran to about 160 pages. It said he had "no hesitation in unambiguously determining that collusion is a significant feature of the Loughinisland murders". He used the definition given by Justice Smithwick, the judge who examined collusion in the killing of two RUC officers, and which the PSNI accepted. His main findings were these:

ul.li: Special Branch had given detectives names and details of people believed responsible within 24 hours, yet there was what he called a "significant delay in arresting suspects" and evidence-gathering chances were lost. One suspect first identified was an RUC informant.
The investigation was marked by "incompetence, indifference and neglect" and by "unexplained delays in arrests", lost forensic opportunities and "inconsistencies or anomalies".

Records on Loughinisland were among those destroyed after asbestos contamination at an Armagh police barracks in 1998. The RUC had kept no inventory of the basement contents, and cleaning the documents was ruled out on cost grounds.

He found no specific intelligence about an intended attack on the bar, and no evidence police had prior knowledge. But he said intelligence was not passed on before the attack, sometimes to protect informants, and that sources were not asked for information that could have prevented attacks such as this one.

He was satisfied that "corrupt relationships existed between members of the security forces in south Down and the UVF unit" to whom police attributed the murders. He also said that despite the failings, many within the RUC and PSNI had worked tirelessly to bring those responsible to justice, and that his investigation was limited by the refusal of a number of key people to speak to his investigators.

content.p: Maguire also stated plainly that the persons responsible for the atrocity were those who entered the bar and fired.

The 2016 report widened the story beyond one pub. It traced two of the weapons connected to the attack, including the main firearm, a VZ58 assault rifle, to a shipment the UVF, UDA and Ulster Resistance had imported in late 1987 and early 1988. Police records, the Ombudsman said, indicated that VZ58 rifles were used in more than 70 murders and attempted murders from March 1988.

Senior figures in the three organisations, among them informants, were never investigated over the importation. Maguire attributed that to a decision by Special Branch not to pass on the intelligence, and called the decision "indefensible". The report also described how a farm in County Armagh belonging to James Mitchell, a former RUC Reserve Constable who had been convicted of terrorist offences in 1980, was identified as a hiding place for weapons. Mitchell, now dead, was warned within two hours of a police stop of cars carrying some of the shipment that his property would be searched, and the remaining weapons were moved. In the press summary the Ombudsman said he could not establish whether an army search the next day was connected.

PSNI Chief Constable George Hamilton accepted the findings and apologised to the families. He said the report made "uncomfortable reading" and that those responsible for collusion "should be held accountable".

In 2017 the Oscar-winning director Alex Gibney released No Stone Unturned, made with the Belfast journalists Trevor Birney and Barry McCaffrey. It examined the police investigation and named one of the alleged killers. The Irish Times reported the film named suspects it said were involved.

On a Friday in August 2018 the two journalists were arrested in a joint operation by the PSNI and Durham police, according to a news agency report, over the suspected theft of material from the Police Ombudsman's office that had been used in the film. Police said the inquiry concerned sensitive material whose theft "potentially puts lives at risk". Birney and McCaffrey said their material came from an anonymous whistleblower. Amnesty International estimated about 100 officers raided the homes and offices, and said the pair were never charged but stayed on bail for about ten months. Gibney said they had been arrested "for doing good, hard-hitting journalism".

In the week before the journalists were released, three senior judges in Belfast, led by Lord Chief Justice Sir Declan Morgan, quashed the search warrants. Morgan called the granting of the warrants "inappropriate". That Monday the Durham chief constable, Mike Barton, said the journalists were no longer suspects and were released from bail. Barton said his officers had acted in good faith.

The Detail later reported that the journalists and their company, Fine Point Films, won more than £800,000 in damages after the High Court found the police had acted unlawfully in raiding their homes and office, and that Chief Constable Simon Byrne apologised. Later still, recordings of the journalists' police interviews, which police had agreed to hand over, arrived blank. The PSNI called it an error and said it was "certainly not intentional"; Birney said he suspected someone had gone out of their way to erase them.

Two retired policemen, Raymond White and Ronald Hawthorne, a former sub-divisional commander, had challenged the 2016 report for years. In 2017 a first hearing found the report procedurally unfair, and the Ombudsman removed references to Hawthorne. A High Court judge refused in November 2018 to quash the report, and the two appealed.

On 18 June 2020, the 26th anniversary of the attack, the Court of Appeal ruled. Morgan said three paragraphs in a summary chapter "overstepped the mark by amounting to findings of criminal offences by members of the police force", because the Ombudsman's role is to investigate and not to adjudicate. But the court upheld the earlier decision not to strike down the public statement, and the families said they were relieved the 2016 report was not quashed. A law-review blog noted that commentators read the same judgment in very different ways.

When the journalists' inquiry was dropped in 2019, Hamilton said the murder investigation "remains open" but that progress depended on new information, and appealed for anyone who knew what happened to come forward. Amnesty said on the 25th anniversary that the best way for police to show they had learned the lessons would be to put the killers behind bars.
